- The ORs interpretation presents the ordinal model estimates as a set of binary logits on outcomes if *y* ≤ *j*
  - These individual binary logits have the same slopes and ORs but the intercepts differ

## Ordinal logit as a set of parallel binary regressions

- The assumption of equal slopes in the ordinal model is interchangeably called:
  - Proportional odds assumption
  - Parallel regression assumption
- Suppose *y* has 4 outcomes (e.g. SD, D, A, SA)
- Create 4 - 1 = 3 binary variables

  B~1~=1 if *y* ≤ 1, else 0

  B~2~=1 if *y* ≤ 2, else 0

  B~3~=1 if *y* ≤ 3, else 0

- Fit three binary logits where both intercepts (α) and coefficients (β) can vary across each model:

$$\begin{aligned} \Pr(B_{1}) &= \Pr(y \leq 1) = F(\alpha_{1} + \beta_{1,1}x_{1} + \beta_{2,1}x_{2}) \\ \Pr(B_{2}) &= \Pr(y \leq 2) = F(\alpha_{2} + \beta_{1,2}x_{1} + \beta_{2,2}x_{2}) \\ \Pr(B_{3}) &= \Pr(y \leq 3) = F(\alpha_{3} + \beta_{1,3}x_{1} + \beta_{2,3}x_{2}) \end{aligned}$$

- Ordinal logit simultaneously fits the equations:

$$\begin{aligned} \Pr(y \leq 1) &= F(\alpha_{1} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{2}) \\ \Pr(y \leq 2) &= F(\alpha_{2} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{2}) \\ \Pr(y \leq 3) &= F(\alpha_{3} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{2}) \end{aligned}$$

  - The β's are constrained to be **identical** in all equations
  - The intercepts (α) vary by cumulative outcome (these are the estimates of the thresholds $\tau$)

#### With and without the parallel regression assumption

## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*Simulate data to show parallel regression assumption
clear
set seed 30004
set obs 2000
matrix P = (1, 0.2 \ 0.2, 1) // Small correlation
corr2data x1 x2, n(2000) cov(P)
gen c = rnormal(0,10)
gen b = c
replace b = 0 in 1/1000
replace b = 1 in 1001/2000
gen y1 = uniform() < invlogit(-3 - 0.15*(c) + 2*(b))
gen y2 = uniform() < invlogit(0 - 0.15*(c) + 2*(b))
gen y3 = uniform() < invlogit( 3 - 0.15*(c) + 2*(b))

gen y1A = uniform() < invlogit(-3 - 0.15*(c) + 2*(b))
gen y2A = uniform() < invlogit(0 - 0.1*(c) + 2*(b))
gen y3A = uniform() < invlogit(3 - 0.3*(c) + 2*(b))

// Parallel Regressions //
qui logit y1 c.c i.b x1 x2
qui margins, at(c=(-60(2)60)) saving(y1, replace)

qui logit y2 c.c i.b x1 x2
qui margins, at(c=(-60(2)60)) saving(y2, replace)

qui logit y3 c.c i.b x1 x2
qui margins, at(c=(-60(2)60)) saving(y3, replace)

combomarginsplot y1 y2 y3, noci ///
    file1opts(msym(none)) file2opts(msym(none)) file3opts(msym(none)) ///
    xlab(-60(10)60) legend(order(1 "Pr y <= 1" 2 "Pr y <= 2" 3 "Pr y <= 3")) ///
    ytitle("Cumulative Probability") title("With Constraint of Parallel Regressions")
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/cda-05-parallel-1.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do>>
// w/o Parallel Regressions //
qui logit y1A c.c i.b x1 x2
qui margins, at(c=(-50(2)50)) saving(y1, replace)

qui logit y2A c.c i.b x1 x2
qui margins, at(c=(-50(2)50)) saving(y2, replace)

qui logit y3A c.c i.b x1 x2
qui margins, at(c=(-50(2)50)) saving(y3, replace)

combomarginsplot y1 y2 y3, noci ///
    file1opts(msym(none)) file2opts(msym(none)) file3opts(msym(none)) ///
    xlab(-50(10)50) legend(order(1 "Pr y <= 1" 2 "Pr y <= 2" 3 "Pr y <= 3")) ///
    ytitle("Cumulative Probability") title("Without Constraint of Parallel Regressions")
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/cda-05-parallel-2.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/cda-05-parallel-1.png){width=80% fig-alt="With the constraint of parallel regressions: three S-shaped cumulative probability curves for Pr(y ≤ 1), Pr(y ≤ 2), and Pr(y ≤ 3) fall from 1 to 0 across c with the same slope, shifted about 20 units apart."}

![](fig/cda-05-parallel-2.png){width=80% fig-alt="Without the constraint of parallel regressions: the three cumulative probability curves fall at different rates; Pr(y ≤ 2) is the flattest and Pr(y ≤ 3) the steepest, so the curves cross."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "With the constraint of parallel regressions: three S-shaped cumulative probability curves for Pr(y ≤ 1), Pr(y ≤ 2), and Pr(y ≤ 3) fall from 1 to 0 across c with the same slope, shifted about 20 units apart."
library(haven)           # import Stata data and labels
library(dplyr)           # data manipulation
library(sjmisc)          # frq() frequency tables
library(ggplot2)         # graphs
library(MASS)            # ordinal logit: polr(); mvrnorm()
library(nnet)            # multinomial logit: multinom()
library(marginaleffects) # predictions and marginal effects
library(brant)           # Brant test: brant()
library(car)             # Anova()
library(suest)           # combine models to compare MEs: suest()
library(cleanplots)      # graph scheme
cleanplots_defaults()

# Simulate data to show parallel regression assumption
# (R's random numbers differ from Stata's, so the estimates differ a little)
set.seed(30004)
n <- 2000
sim <- as.data.frame(mvrnorm(n, mu = c(0, 0), Sigma = matrix(c(1, .2, .2, 1), 2),
  empirical = TRUE))  # x1 and x2 with a small correlation
names(sim) <- c("x1", "x2")
sim <- sim |>
  mutate(c = rnorm(n, 0, 10),
    b = rep(0:1, each = n / 2),
    y1 = as.numeric(runif(n) < plogis(-3 - 0.15 * c + 2 * b)),
    y2 = as.numeric(runif(n) < plogis(0 - 0.15 * c + 2 * b)),
    y3 = as.numeric(runif(n) < plogis(3 - 0.15 * c + 2 * b)),
    y1A = as.numeric(runif(n) < plogis(-3 - 0.15 * c + 2 * b)),
    y2A = as.numeric(runif(n) < plogis(0 - 0.1 * c + 2 * b)),
    y3A = as.numeric(runif(n) < plogis(3 - 0.3 * c + 2 * b)))

# Average predicted Pr(y = 1) from a binary logit at values of c
cum_pr <- function(outcome, cvalues) {
  m <- glm(reformulate(c("c", "b", "x1", "x2"), outcome), data = sim, family = binomial)
  avg_predictions(m, by = "c", newdata = datagrid(c = cvalues, grid_type = "counterfactual"))
}
cum_labels <- c("Pr y <= 1", "Pr y <= 2", "Pr y <= 3")

# Parallel Regressions
parallel <- bind_rows(lapply(c("y1", "y2", "y3"), cum_pr, cvalues = seq(-60, 60, 2)),
  .id = "outcome")

ggplot(parallel, aes(x = c, y = estimate, color = outcome)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_discrete(labels = cum_labels) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-60, 60, 10)) +
  labs(title = "With Constraint of Parallel Regressions",
    y = "Cumulative Probability", color = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Without the constraint of parallel regressions: the three cumulative probability curves fall at different rates; Pr(y ≤ 2) is the flattest and Pr(y ≤ 3) the steepest, so the curves cross."
# w/o Parallel Regressions
nonparallel <- bind_rows(lapply(c("y1A", "y2A", "y3A"), cum_pr, cvalues = seq(-50, 50, 2)),
  .id = "outcome")

ggplot(nonparallel, aes(x = c, y = estimate, color = outcome)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_discrete(labels = cum_labels) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-50, 50, 10)) +
  labs(title = "Without Constraint of Parallel Regressions",
    y = "Cumulative Probability", color = NULL)
```

:::

Is the slope for Pr(*y* ≤ 2) significantly different from Pr(*y* ≤ 3)? Pr(*y* ≤ 1)? Etc.

### Ordinality assumption revisited

- To begin this section, I emphasized the ordinality assumption is about **the relationship between the IVs and the DVs**---it is an assumption about the model, not just about the DV
- Even when your DV is clearly an inherently ordinal DV (e.g., educational degree attainment)---this does not mean your **model** will meet the ordinality assumption
- Consider the graph above: this plots the cumulative probabilities across the range of a continuous IV
  - Some IVs may produce ordinal relationships with the DV
  - Some IVs may not
- Thus, **a DV itself can never satisfy the ordinality assumption** of the model
  - E.g., A DV may pass the assumption in one model or sample, but not an alternative with different IVs, or in a different sample

### Formal tests of parallel regressions

- The **Brant test** determines if the coefficients from individual binary logits equal those from the ordinal logit model where they are all constrained to be equal
  - In Stata, **spost13** command **brant** will calculate this for you; both for each individual IV and an overall test for the model; in R, package [**brant**](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/brant/versions/0.3-0/topics/brant)
- Tests often reject the parallel regression assumption
  - In my experience, they are very sensitive to even minor deviations from perfectly parallel regressions
- If rejected, verify the consequences of the assumption by comparing predictions from the ordinal model with a model that does not impose the parallel regression assumption (e.g., multinomial logit)
  - I would not publish results from ordinal logit when tests indicate a violation of the parallel regression assumption **unless** I can provide explicit evidence it does not bias conclusions

### Brant test of the parallel regression assumption

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss", clear

lab def likertlab 1"StrAgree" 2"Agree" 3"Disagree" 4"StrDisag"
lab val pillok likertlab

gen religous = attend
lab var religous "Religious Attendee"
recode religous 0/3 = 0 4/8 = 1
lab def religlab 0"Not Religious" 1"Religious"
lab val religous religlab

drop if year < 1986
drop if missing(pillok, year1972, religous, college, age, woman, race3, faminc)

qui ologit pillok c.year1972 c.age i.woman i.religous ///
    i.college i.race3 c.faminc, or
est store opmod

// Test the parallel regression assumption
brant
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
gss <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss.dta")

# Religious attendee = attends about once a month or more
gss <- gss |>
  mutate(religous = case_when(attend <= 3 ~ 0, attend >= 4 ~ 1)) |>
  filter(year >= 1986)

# Keep model variables; drop any missing data
gss <- gss[c("pillok", "year1972", "religous", "college", "age", "woman", "race3", "faminc")]
gss <- gss[complete.cases(gss), ]

# Ordinal DV as a factor with short labels; binary/nominal variables as factors
gss <- gss |>
  mutate(pillok = factor(pillok, levels = 1:4,
      labels = c("StrAgree", "Agree", "Disagree", "StrDisag")),
    religous = factor(religous, labels = c("Not Religious", "Religious")),
    across(c(college, woman, race3), as_factor),
    year1972 = as.numeric(year1972)) |>
  droplevels()

opmod <- polr(pillok ~ year1972 + age + woman + religous + college + race3 + faminc,
  data = gss, Hess = TRUE)

# Test the parallel regression assumption
brant(opmod)
```

:::

> *A Brant test indicates that the model violates the parallel regression assumption of the ordinal logit model (p \< 0.001). Age, gender, religiosity, education, and race all have relationships with views of teenage birth control that may not be strictly ordered in nature (all five individual tests p \< 0.05).*

## Comparing ordinal and nominal predictions

- Before blindly accepting or rejecting the ordinal logit model based on a test of parallel regressions, you should also examine whether predictions from the ordinal model differ importantly from those in a model that **does not impose ordinality**

#### Effects of assuming wrong level of measurement

| **Model choice** (assumed level of DV for analysis) | **True level of DV:** Nominal | Ordinal | Continuous\* |
|:------|:------:|:------:|:------:|
| Nominal | **Ideal** | *Inefficient* | *Inefficient* |
| Ordinal | ***Biased*** | **Ideal** | *Inefficient* |
| Continuous | ***Biased*** | ***Biased*** | **Ideal** |

\*I am not distinguishing between interval and ratio variables here

- If outcome is ordinal and model is nominal, it is inefficient, but a safe choice
  - If outcome is nominal but model is ordinal, you will have **biased estimates**
- Here I compare ordinal logit to multinomial logit
  - You could also compare predictions to those from the generalized ordered logit model (see [Section 5.6](5-6-generalized-ordered-logit.qmd))

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[5.4.e] ordinal logit and [5.4.a] multinomial logit predicted probabilities of each view by survey year side by side: the two models give nearly the same, nearly flat lines."
#| fig-width: 9.5
# Same model with multinomial logit
mpmod <- multinom(pillok ~ year1972 + age + woman + religous + college + race3 + faminc,
  data = gss, trace = FALSE)

# Average predictions from both models at values of an IV
pr_both <- function(variable, values) {
  grid <- do.call(datagrid, c(list(newdata = gss, grid_type = "counterfactual"),
    setNames(list(values), variable)))
  bind_rows(
    "Ordinal Logit" = avg_predictions(opmod, by = c(variable, "group"), newdata = grid),
    "Multinomial Logit" = avg_predictions(mpmod, by = c(variable, "group"), newdata = grid),
    .id = "model") |>
    mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("Ordinal Logit", "Multinomial Logit")))
}

# 5.4.e and 5.4.a
ggplot(pr_both("year1972", 14:49), aes(x = year1972, y = estimate, color = group)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = group), alpha = .2, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(18, 28, 38, 49), labels = c("1990", "2000", "2010", "2021")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .5, .1), limits = c(0, .5)) +
  labs(x = "GSS Survey Year", y = "Pr(View of Birth Control for Teenagers)",
    color = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[5.4.f] ordinal logit and [5.4.b] multinomial logit predicted probabilities of each view by age side by side: both show strongly agree falling and strongly disagree rising with age; the multinomial model has disagree rising faster and strongly disagree rising slower than the ordinal model."
#| fig-width: 9.5
# 5.4.f and 5.4.b
ggplot(pr_both("age", seq(18, 90, 4)), aes(x = age, y = estimate, color = group)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = group), alpha = .2, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(18, 88, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .5, .1), limits = c(0, .5)) +
  labs(x = "Age in Years", y = "Pr(View of Birth Control for Teenagers)",
    color = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[5.4.g] ordinal logit and [5.4.c] multinomial logit average marginal effects of gender on each view side by side: both have positive effects for strongly agree and agree and negative effects for disagree and strongly disagree, but the multinomial model's effect for disagree is larger and for strongly disagree smaller."
#| fig-width: 9.5
# AMEs from both models
me_both <- function(variable) {
  bind_rows(
    "Ordinal Logit" = avg_comparisons(opmod, variables = variable),
    "Multinomial Logit" = avg_comparisons(mpmod, variables = variable),
    .id = "model") |>
    mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("Ordinal Logit", "Multinomial Logit")))
}

ame_plot <- function(mes, ytitle, ylimits) {
  ggplot(mes, aes(x = group, y = estimate)) +
    geom_col(width = .6, fill = "lightblue") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = .1, color = "gray30") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    facet_wrap(~ model) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Strongly\nAgree", "Agree", "Disagree", "Strongly\nDisagree")) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = ylimits) +
    labs(x = "Teenagers Should Have Birth Control?", y = ytitle)
}

# 5.4.g and 5.4.c
ame_plot(me_both("woman"), "AME of Gender (Woman = 1)", c(-.1, .1))
```

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[5.4.h] ordinal logit and [5.4.d] multinomial logit average marginal effects of religiosity on each view side by side: both are negative for strongly agree and agree and positive for disagree and strongly disagree; the multinomial model has a larger negative effect for agree and a larger positive effect for strongly disagree."
#| fig-width: 9.5
# 5.4.h and 5.4.d
ame_plot(me_both("religous"), "AME of Religiosity (Religious = 1)", c(-.2, .2))
```

:::

### Comparing model predicted probabilities

- The plots above compare AMEs and ranges of predictions for particular independent variables.
- It can also be informative to examine predicted probabilities for individual observations
  - E.g., What is the Pr(Agree) for observation #103 when using **ologit** vs **mlogit**?

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
// 5.4.i - Compare predictions for individual obs
est restore mpmod
predict mpr1 mpr2 mpr3 mpr4

est restore opmod
predict opr1 opr2 opr3 opr4

scatter mpr1 opr1, jitter(2) xlab(0(.1).6) ylab(0(.1).6) msize(vsmall) ///
    xtitle("Pr(StrAgree) from Ordinal Logit") ytitle("Pr(StrAgree) Multinomial Logit") ///
    saving(pr1.gph, replace)
scatter mpr2 opr2, jitter(2) xlab(0(.1).6) ylab(0(.1).6) msize(vsmall) ///
    xtitle("Pr(Agree) from Ordinal Logit") ytitle("Pr(Agree) Multinomial Logit") ///
    saving(pr2.gph, replace)
scatter mpr3 opr3, jitter(2) xlab(0(.1).6) ylab(0(.1).6) msize(vsmall) ///
    xtitle("Pr(Disagree) from Ordinal Logit") ytitle("Pr(Disagree) Multinomial Logit") ///
    saving(pr3.gph, replace)
scatter mpr4 opr4, jitter(2) xlab(0(.1).6) ylab(0(.1).6) msize(vsmall) ///
    xtitle("Pr(StrDisagree) from Ordinal Logit") ytitle("Pr(StrDisagree) Multinomial Logit") ///
    saving(pr4.gph, replace)

graph combine pr1.gph pr2.gph pr3.gph pr4.gph, ///
    title("[5.4.i] Predicted Probabilities from Multinomial Logit (y-axis)" ///
        "vs Ordinal Logit (x-axis)", size(medsmall))
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/cda-05_04_5-orm_vs_mlm.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/cda-05_04_5-orm_vs_mlm.png){width=80% fig-alt="[5.4.i] Four scatterplots of each observation's predicted probability from the multinomial logit (y-axis) against the ordinal logit (x-axis): strongly agree and strongly disagree fall close to a straight line, while agree and disagree spread out more, especially at the higher ordinal-logit predictions."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[5.4.i] Four scatterplots of each observation's predicted probability from the multinomial logit (y-axis) against the ordinal logit (x-axis): strongly agree and strongly disagree fall close to a straight line, while agree and disagree spread out more, especially at the higher ordinal-logit predictions."
#| fig-height: 7
# 5.4.i - Compare predictions for individual obs
pr_obs <- data.frame(outcome = rep(levels(gss$pillok), each = nrow(gss)),
  multinomial = as.vector(predict(mpmod, type = "probs")),
  ordinal = as.vector(predict(opmod, type = "probs"))) |>
  mutate(outcome = factor(outcome, levels = levels(gss$pillok)))

ggplot(pr_obs, aes(x = ordinal, y = multinomial)) +
  geom_point(size = .3, alpha = .3) +
  facet_wrap(~ outcome) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .6, .1), limits = c(0, .6)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .6, .1), limits = c(0, .6)) +
  labs(title = "[5.4.i] Predicted Probabilities from Multinomial Logit (y-axis) vs Ordinal Logit (x-axis)",
    x = "Pr from Ordinal Logit", y = "Pr from Multinomial Logit") +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
```

:::

Where do the ordinal and multinomial models differ the most? Why?

### Example: Political party affiliation\*

- GSS 2010 -- 2021
  - DV: Political party affiliation
  - IVs: Age and gender
  - Control variables: education, parental status, marital status, family income, employment status, US region, and survey year

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*2010 - 2021 GSS
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss", clear
drop if year < 2010

drop if missing(partyid5, woman, edyrs, age, parent, married, ///
    faminc, employed, region4, year)

fre partyid5
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
party <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss.dta")
party <- party |> filter(year >= 2010)

# Keep model variables; drop any missing data
party <- party[c("partyid5", "woman", "edyrs", "age", "parent", "married", "faminc",
  "employed", "region4", "year")]
party <- party[complete.cases(party), ]

frq(party$partyid5)

# Outcome as a factor (and an ordered factor for polr); IVs as factors
party <- party |>
  mutate(partyid5 = as_factor(partyid5),
    party_ord = ordered(partyid5),
    across(c(woman, parent, married, employed, region4), as_factor),
    year = factor(year)) |>
  droplevels() |>
  as.data.frame()
```

:::

\*This example is an updated example of that shown in [Long and Freese 2014](https://www.stata-press.com/books/regression-models-categorical-dependent-variables/) who use data from the 1992 National Election Study; this specific example from [Mize, Doan, and Long 2019](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0081175019852763)

#### Ordinal logit: DV = political party affiliation

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
///////////////////
// Ordinal Logit //
///////////////////
ologit partyid5 c.age i.woman c.edyrs i.parent i.married ///
    c.faminc i.employed i.region4 i.year, or
est store oparty
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
# Ordinal Logit
oparty <- polr(party_ord ~ age + woman + edyrs + parent + married + faminc + employed +
  region4 + year, data = party, Hess = TRUE)
summary(oparty)

# Odds ratios
exp(coef(oparty))
```

:::

- In terms of the coefficients (*y\**):
  - Age has no effect on the odds of political party affiliation
  - Women are less likely to identify as more Republican

#### AMEs from ordinal logit model

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
mchange age woman, amount(sd)
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
# AMEs (mchange's +SD change starts at each observation's value)
avg_comparisons(oparty, variables = list(age = sd(party$age)))
avg_comparisons(oparty, variables = "woman")
```

:::

- In terms of AMEs:
  - Age has no effect on the probability of identifying with any of the five political party affiliations
  - Gender has a significant effect on the probability of identifying with each of the five political party affiliations

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[5.4.i] Ordinal logit predicted probabilities of each party affiliation by age from 18 to 93: all five lines are flat (Democrat about 0.30, Republican about 0.22, Strong Dem and Independent about 0.18, Strong Repub about 0.11)."
# Colors and line types for the party affiliation categories
party_colors <- c("blue", "lightblue", "gray60", "#FF8080", "red")
party_lines <- c("solid", "dashed", "solid", "dashed", "solid")

party_plot <- function(model, ages, title, ylimits = c(0, .4)) {
  pr <- avg_predictions(model, by = c("age", "group"),
    newdata = datagrid(age = ages, grid_type = "counterfactual"))
  ggplot(pr, aes(x = age, y = estimate, color = group, linetype = group)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    scale_color_manual(values = party_colors) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = party_lines) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = ylimits) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Age in Years", y = "Pr(Party Affiliation)",
      color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
    theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
}

# 5.4.i
party_plot(oparty, seq(18, 93, 5),
  "[5.4.i] Ordinal Logit: Predicted Probabilities of Political Party Affiliation")
```

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[5.4.k] Ordinal logit predicted probabilities of each party affiliation for impossible ages from -30,000 to 30,000: Pr(Strong Dem) falls from near 1 to near 0 and Pr(Strong Repub) rises from near 0 to near 1, with the middle categories peaking in between, which shows the ordinal functional form."
# 5.4.k
party_plot(oparty, seq(-30000, 30000, 1000),
  "[5.4.k] Ordinal Logit: Predicted Probabilities of Political Party Affiliation", c(0, 1))
```

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[5.4.m] Bar chart of the ordinal logit average marginal effects of gender (woman = 1) on each party affiliation: about 0.04 for Strong Dem, 0.03 for Democrat, -0.01 for Independent, -0.03 for Republican, and -0.03 for Strong Repub."
# 5.4.m
me_party_plot <- function(model, title) {
  ggplot(avg_comparisons(model, variables = "woman"),
    aes(x = group, y = estimate, fill = group)) +
    geom_col(width = .7) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = .1, color = "gray40") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = party_colors) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = round(seq(-.075, .075, .025), 3), limits = c(-.075, .075)) +
    labs(title = title,
      subtitle = "Effects Above Zero Indicate That Political View is More Likely for Women",
      x = "Political Party Affiliation", y = "Effect of Gender (Woman = 1)", fill = NULL) +
    theme(plot.title.position = "plot", axis.text.x = element_blank())
}

me_party_plot(oparty, "[5.4.m] Ordinal Logit: Average Marginal Effects of Gender")
```

### Brant test of parallel regressions

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
est restore oparty
brant
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
brant(oparty)
```

:::

> *A Brant test indicates that the model violates the parallel regression assumption of the ordinal logit model (p \< 0.001). Both focal variables of age and gender have relationships with political party affiliation that are not strictly ordered in nature.*

### Multinomial logit model for political party affiliation

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
///////////////////////
// Multinomial Logit //
///////////////////////
qui mlogit partyid5 c.age i.woman c.edyrs i.parent i.married ///
    c.faminc i.employed i.region4 i.year
est store mparty

mlogtest
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
# Multinomial Logit
mparty <- multinom(partyid5 ~ age + woman + edyrs + parent + married + faminc +
  employed + region4 + year, data = party, Hess = TRUE, trace = FALSE)

# Likelihood-ratio tests (region4 and year are each tested as one variable)
Anova(mparty, type = 2)
```

:::

- In terms of the coefficients:
  - Age has a significant effect
  - Gender has a significant effect

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Ordinal logit and multinomial logit predicted probabilities of party affiliation by age side by side: the ordinal model's lines are flat, while the multinomial model shows Strong Dem and Strong Repub rising and Democrat and Independent falling with age."
#| fig-width: 9.5
# Predictions from both models side by side
pr_party <- bind_rows(
  "Ordinal Logit" = avg_predictions(oparty, by = c("age", "group"),
    newdata = datagrid(age = seq(18, 93, 5), grid_type = "counterfactual")),
  "Multinomial Logit" = avg_predictions(mparty, by = c("age", "group"),
    newdata = datagrid(age = seq(18, 93, 5), grid_type = "counterfactual")),
  .id = "model") |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("Ordinal Logit", "Multinomial Logit")))

ggplot(pr_party, aes(x = age, y = estimate, color = group, linetype = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_color_manual(values = party_colors) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = party_lines) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, .4)) +
  labs(x = "Age in Years", y = "Pr(Party Affiliation)", color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Ordinal logit and multinomial logit average marginal effects of gender side by side: the ordinal model has effects that shift steadily from positive for Strong Dem to negative for Strong Repub, while the multinomial model's largest effects are for Strong Dem (positive) and Republican (negative), with Strong Repub only slightly negative."
#| fig-width: 9.5
# AMEs of gender from both models side by side
me_party <- bind_rows(
  "Ordinal Logit" = avg_comparisons(oparty, variables = "woman"),
  "Multinomial Logit" = avg_comparisons(mparty, variables = "woman"),
  .id = "model") |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("Ordinal Logit", "Multinomial Logit")))

ggplot(me_party, aes(x = group, y = estimate, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = .7) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = .1, color = "gray40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = party_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = round(seq(-.075, .075, .025), 3), limits = c(-.075, .075)) +
  labs(x = "Political Party Affiliation", y = "Effect of Gender (Woman = 1)", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_blank())
```

## Testing predictions and effects across models

- The comparisons of the ordinal and nominal model in this section are informal
  - I.e., I did not conduct any significance tests as to whether the predictions and/or MEs were different across the two models
- [Mize, Doan, and Long (2019)](/research/mize_doan_long_2019_SM.qmd) develop a method that can be used to test for differences across the ordinal and multinomial logit models (see example 6.5 in the article)
  - In Stata, the [**mecompare**](/software/mecompare/examples/model-types.qmd) command automates these tests
  - In R, use [**suest**](/software/suest_r/articles/model-types.qmd) to combine the two model's estimates, and [**avg_comparisons**](https://marginaleffects.com/man/r/comparisons.html) to calculate the MEs to compare

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*mecompare with two models() combines estimates using SUEST and calculates
**difference in MEs across models
mecompare age, models(oparty mparty) amount(sd)
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
# Center changes in continuous IVs on each observation's value (as mecompare does)
options(marginaleffects_contrast_direction = "center")

# suest combines the estimates of the two models
party_suest <- suest(oparty, mparty, model_names = c("oparty", "mparty"))

me_age <- avg_comparisons(party_suest, variables = list(age = sd(party$age)),
  newdata = party)
me_age

# Difference between the models for each outcome: oparty - mparty
model_diffs <- function(x) {
  data.frame(term = sub("^oparty::", "", x$group[1:5]),
    estimate = x$estimate[1:5] - x$estimate[6:10])
}
hypotheses(me_age, hypothesis = model_diffs)
```

:::

> *The average marginal effect of age is significantly different across the ordinal and nominal model for the probability of identifying as a strong Democrat, a Democrat, an independent, and a strong Republican (all cross-model differences p \< .001). The models suggest similar non-significant effects of age on the probability of identifying as a Republican (cross-model difference p = n.s.).*

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*binary IV woman
mecompare woman, models(oparty mparty)
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
# binary IV woman
me_woman <- avg_comparisons(party_suest, variables = "woman", newdata = party)
me_woman

diff_woman <- hypotheses(me_woman, hypothesis = model_diffs)
diff_woman
```

:::

> *The cross-model differences for the effect of gender are not significant for strong Democrat, Democrat, and independent (all cross-model differences p \> .05). However, the models differ in the size of the gender gap for Republican and strong Republican (both cross-model differences p \< .01).*

### Omnibus tests of difference

- Similar to the variable-specific Brant test, we can obtain a single omnibus test of whether the two models' marginal effects differ or not
  - This obviates the multiple hypothesis testing issue
  - To do so, test if all of the differences are simultaneously equal to zero with **metest** (**\#**s refer to the ME \# column of **mecompare**)
    - To specify an integer, not a ME, use a **\#** (so **#0** = zero)

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
qui mecompare woman, models(oparty mparty)
metest (3 = #0) (6 = #0) (9 = #0) (12 = #0) (15 = #0), rowname("All differences = 0")
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
# The five differences sum to zero, so a joint test of any four of them
# tests all differences = 0
hypotheses(diff_woman, joint = 1:4, joint_test = "chisq")
```

:::

> *Overall, the ordinal and nominal models differ in the marginal effects of gender (omnibus test p \< .001). This suggests the ordinal model's assumptions do not hold for gender and are biasing its estimates of gender's marginal effects.*
